analysis.one_liner: Requires federal wildlife and wetlands regulators to compensate property owners when rules cut a land's value in half.
analysis.headline: With 165 cosponsors and broad bipartisan backing, the bill never reached a House floor vote; three committees kept it, and the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995 without action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force federal agencies enforcing the Endangered Species Act and Clean Water Act wetland permits to minimize the burden on private landowners, get written consent before entering their property, let them review and dispute data collected there, and give them administrative appeals of permit denials and penalties. Its core provision would entitle landowners to taxpayer compensation if a final agency decision cuts the affected property's fair market value or viable use by 50 percent or more, with offers to buy the land or pay the difference, and binding arbitration if the owner rejects both. The Senate never considered a companion measure and the House committees never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Private landowners whose property is restricted to protect endangered species habitat or wetlands—farmers, timber owners, and developers whose land loses value or use. Ordinary citizens gain if the compensation requirement makes agencies weigh the economic cost before restricting land, but also gain from the consent, data-review, and appeal rights.

how_it_helps.text: Entitles an owner to compensation when a final agency action deprives them of 50 percent or more of the affected property's fair market value or economically viable use.

Requires written owner consent before a federal agency may enter private property to collect information, and gives the owner the right to review and dispute that data before it is used to enforce the Endangered Species Act or the wetlands permitting program.

Creates administrative appeal rights for wetlands and endangered-species decisions—including jurisdiction determinations, permit denials, permit terms, penalties, and restoration orders—with the appeal heard by a different official near the property.
Directs agencies to comply with state and tribal laws and to administer both environmental acts in the manner that least affects private property owners' constitutional and legal rights.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who would fund buyouts of restricted land or pay the value reduction, and therefore all who benefit from species and wetland protections carried out on private land—largely through the Treasury rather than as a direct user fee. Industries that benefit from the restrictions—developers, extractive users, agribusiness on converted land—would gain cheaply obtained waivers or compensation.

drawbacks.text: Paying landowners for every major restriction could make protecting habitat and wetlands on private land prohibitively expensive, effectively weakening those protections, and requires new federal spending without an offset.

The bill does not change the underlying conservation standards; it adds process, data-privacy limits on site inspections, and a compensation trigger, leaving open whether compliance costs or the risk of a large payout claim would chill enforcement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The owner-protection provisions are real and address a genuine grievance, but the compensation mandate is the bill's core: any major use restriction automatically triggers a payout offer, so the federal government would face large, recurring costs and agencies would have a strong fiscal reason to avoid designating protections that trigger compensation. It buys landowner fairness partly by making environmental protection on private land more expensive to the public.

outcome.mechanism: Three House committees received the bill; none reported it out, no floor vote ever happened, and the 103rd Congress ended without either chamber acting on it.

narrative.text: Introduced on February 23, 1994, and jointly referred to the Merchant Marine and Fisheries, Public Works and Transportation, and Judiciary Committees.
Gained 165 cosponsors, split 127 Republicans and 38 Democrats.
Subcommittees in all three committees held it during 1994; the Justice Department later provided unfavorable executive comment.

On June 29, 1994, sponsor Tauzin filed a discharge petition to force the bill out of committee; the petition did not succeed, and the bill never received a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody in the general public gained—the bill simply died. The absence of the compensation mandate meant no new federal payout obligations, so the Treasury and environmental-protection goals were unaffected; the bill's backers got nothing, and landowner grievances went unaddressed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the bill died unaddressed

for.name: W. J. (Billy) Tauzin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, promoted it in floor remarks, and filed a discharge petition to force a vote.

for.name: The bill's 165 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in large numbers—127 Republicans and 38 Democrats—signaling broad bipartisan support that never translated into committee action.

against.name: House committees of jurisdiction
against.role: Merchant Marine and Fisheries, Public Works and Transportation, and Judiciary Committees
against.what_they_did: Held the bill in subcommittee for the entire session and never reported it or scheduled a vote, effectively killing it.

against.name: Department of Justice
against.what_they_did: Submitted unfavorable executive comment on the bill in June 1994.

against.name: Environmental and conservation groups
against.what_they_did: Bills of this type were strongly opposed by conservation groups, who argued the compensation mandate would gut habitat and wetland protection on private land.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship split 127 Republicans and 38 Democrats, but it was a heavily one-sided bipartisan coalition rather than a party-line fight, and the bill died in committee without a recorded vote.

industries.industry: Landowners with ESA or wetland restrictions (farm, timber, and real estate interests)
industries.note: These owners would gain compensation for use restrictions and process rights, which directly benefits land-heavy private interests including large landholders and developers.
Would gain an easier path around wetland and habitat restrictions, either by compensation payouts to landowners or administrative appeals, reducing the cost of development on protected land.
Would bear the cost of buyouts or value-reduction payments, with no dedicated funding source, meaning the public absorbs the bill's fiscal burden.
